To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SOCS-1/3 are up-regulated in the livers of obese mice and men, and that this up-regulation contributes to insulin resistance and hepatic steatogenesis.

the suppressors of cytokines SOCS-1 (and to a greater extent SOCS-3) are important mediators of the metabolic syndrome in obesity, by down-regulating insulin signaling, and by up-regulating SREBP- 1, which is a key regulator of fatty-acid synthesis.

the SOCS family of cytokine inhibitors are important mediators of hepatic insulin resistance and steatosis, and that they may be important targets for the treatment of insulin resistance and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of insulin resistance and hepatic steatogenesis.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the pathogenesis of obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
the molecular mechanisms of the pathogenesis of obesity, insulin resistance, and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SOCS-1/3 is a key regulator of insulin resistance and hepatic steatogenesis.
SOCS proteins, especially SOCS-1, are involved in the development of insulin resistance and fatty liver, but that they are not causative factors in the development of obesity.
the increased SOCS proteins in the metabolic syndrome may be a double-edged sword.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metabolic syndrome is caused by the imbalance of the two signaling pathways, the JAK/STAT and the JAK/IRS, which are antagonized by SOCS proteins.
SOCS-1/3 are the molecular link between cytokine signaling and metabolic signaling in liver.
SOCS proteins, which are induced in the liver by inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha, inhibit the insulin signal transduction by down-regulating tyrosine phosphorylated IRS proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic syndrome is a disease of chronic inflammation and that inflammation is a major contributor to the development of the metabolic syndrome.

obesity and insulin resistance are associated with increased expression of SOCS proteins in liver, which down-regulates tyrosine phosphorylated IRS proteins and up-regulates expression of SREBPs, leading to hepatic steatostis and hypertriglyeridemia.
SOCS proteins are important in the pathogenesis of the Metabolic Syndrome by concordantly down-regulating cytokine and insulin signaling.
